sections.theory:
Lingkuan Gorge

[Summary — the full story by Tu Peng-Cheng is a modern copyrighted text (English translation); read it in the printed textbook, pp. 131–134.]

On a snowy evening the narrator, chief of a railway project’s Materials Department, has walked forty kilometres along the route of a future railway. Entering Lingkuan Gorge, where the sun never shines, he finds construction going on day and night — generators, cement-mixers, lights and overhead cables loaded with materials.

Cold, hungry and having fallen in the dark, he decides to rest until morning and climbs to a workers’ cave in the cliff-side. Inside, a small boy of seven or eight sits in the doorway, his face in his hands, watching the opposite cliff through a gap in the curtain; his baby sister sleeps on the bed.

The boy, Cheng-yu, proudly insists that he is “somebody” and introduces his sister Pao-cheng. Like many children of construction workers, they are named after the railway projects where they were born.

When the narrator teases him about the snow, Cheng-yu is offended; he explains that his father, who “opens up mountains,” will have to stop work if it keeps snowing, and he keeps watching the work site opposite.
